title: Robber Barons!
summary: Josh and Chuck discuss the Gilded Age and the "robber barons" of late nineteenth-century America: the shift from an agrarian to industrial economy, steel and railroads, wealth inequality statistics, the etymology of "robber baron" in medieval Rhine River tolls, and profiles of Cornelius Vanderbilt, J.P. Morgan, Andrew Carnegie, and John D. Rockefeller, including the Homestead Strike, Standard Oil's railroad rebates, and their philanthropy. They also touch on conservative and liberal views of inequality and a listener email about the word "cannabis" versus "marijuana." The episode opens and closes with book pre-order promotion.
topics: Mark Twain The Gilded Age novel

segments.title: Book pre-order announcement
segments.summary: Hosts promote pre-ordering their book Stuff You Should Know: An Incomplete Compendium of Mostly Interesting Things and uploading a receipt for a custom poster.

segments.title: Opening banter and framing robber barons
segments.summary: Hosts introduce robber barons as polarizing figures and banter about conservative and liberal views of human imperfection and government regulation.

segments.title: What the Gilded Age was
segments.summary: The Gilded Age is defined as roughly the late nineteenth century, from the end of the Civil War to the first decade of the 1900s, marked by rapid shift from agrarian to industrial economy with little federal regulation, while government engaged in corporate welfare.

segments.title: Steel, railroads and industrial growth
segments.summary: Henry Bessemer's cheap steel process enabled railroad expansion, letting regional industries reach national markets. The War of 1812 and the Civil War are cited as factors in the nation's industrial growth, and the era's political engagement is discussed.

segments.title: Mid-episode tangent and book plug
segments.summary: A brief tangent about Happy Days and a repeat of the book pre-order plug.

segments.title: Mark Twain's The Gilded Age and wealth inequality
segments.summary: Mark Twain co-wrote the 1873 satire The Gilded Age, which named the era. The hosts cite 1890 statistics showing the top one percent held about 51 percent of wealth, and discuss inequality criticism.

segments.title: Origin of the term robber baron
segments.summary: The term traces to medieval robber barons on the Rhine who set up tolls at narrow gorges, such as after Emperor Frederick III died in 1250. The term was applied to American tycoons, notably in an 1870 Atlantic article.

segments.title: Cornelius Vanderbilt
segments.summary: Vanderbilt started with ferry boats at age fourteen, broke Robert Fulton's steamship ferry monopoly, moved into railroads, manipulated the Harlem Railroad stock, consolidated New York to Chicago lines, and later funded Grand Central Depot and Vanderbilt University.

segments.title: J.P. Morgan and horizontal integration
segments.summary: J.P. Morgan built an investment bank and used horizontal integration and Morganization to consolidate industries by buying competitors and undercutting holdouts. Teddy Roosevelt's antitrust action against Northern Securities followed, and Morgan's labor practices are criticized.

segments.title: Andrew Carnegie and the Homestead Strike
segments.summary: Carnegie rose from poverty in Scotland to dominate steel. In 1892 the Homestead Strike turned violent after Pinkerton agents were brought in; the National Guard was called and Carnegie's involvement is discussed. Carnegie's philanthropy, especially libraries, is noted.

segments.title: John D. Rockefeller and Standard Oil
segments.summary: Rockefeller's Standard Oil controlled most of the oil market through railroad rebates and penalties on competitors. He was a major philanthropist, funding the University of Chicago and Spelman. The hosts compare historic robber barons to modern billionaires and discuss living standards.

segments.title: Listener mail on cannabis terminology
segments.summary: Listener Jack Glick writes that the Canadian government refers to the plant as cannabis rather than marijuana due to racist associations.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts close with the usual sign-off and the email address for listener mail.
